segments.text: Hello and welcome to this week's Health Report with me, Norman Swan. Today, sleepless in cyberspace, losing sleep over your gut, a warning for shift workers about late night snacks, and how a promising young broadcaster can be turned into a blithering idiot.
But I want to start with an important paper in this week's Medical Journal of Australia.
Said against what anecdotally is a growing number of people being told that their fatigue,
mental fogginess, joint pains and other symptoms are due to chronic Lyme disease,
the paper concluded that there is in fact no Lyme disease in Australia,
that is apart from people who might have caught it on a trip overseas.
Lyme disease is spread by tick bites from infected animals like deer in the Northern Hemisphere,
where there are hundreds of thousands of cases each year.
The symptoms are a rash at the site of the bite, joint pains, headaches and malaise, all treatable with antibiotics.
People diagnosed with chronic Lyme disease in Australia are given long courses of often toxic antibiotics,
so it's important to be sure that the diagnosis is real.
Peter Collignon is an infectious disease physician at the Australian National University and was the lead author on the paper.
Welcome to the Health Report.
Thank you for having me.
You're trying to prove a negative here, aren't you, Peter? It's a bit hard to do.
Well, it is a bit hard. I mean, you can't absolutely say that there's no Lyme disease in Australia.
But what we can say is that we've looked extensively for decades for the bacteria in ticks, in people, in animals,
and we have not been able to find it and grow it, nor reproducibly find the DNA.
Now, that's not to say that ticks may not carry a whole lot of other viruses, bacteria, even fungi that might cause problems to people.
and we actually know ticks carry things like rickettsia, for instance,
people, typhus-like illnesses, etc.
But for the specific syndrome of chronic Lyme disease,
we don't have evidence that that particular Borrelia
that causes that of bacteria is present in Australia.
And that's particularly problematic
because some people are almost demanding months of intravenous antibiotics
with particularly an antibiotic called trocheftroaxone
that causes not only harm to themselves,
that harm to the rest of society because of antibiotic resistance
and, in fact, because of the economic cost of therapy that's inappropriate.
But people say, well, look, my doctor sent my tests off to the local pathology lab
and it came back negative,
but when my sample was sent off to Germany or the United States,
it came back positive, so the local pathologists are incompetent.
Well, one of the things is people can have tests that are positive even here,
antibody tests, but they have, and notoriously can have some false positives.
The ones that are important are the PCR test, the ones that detect the nuclear material, or culture.
The ones that are in dispute are usually the PCR test, finding the DNA makeup.
But the problem with that is even in Australia there's some laboratories that say they've found it,
but it's not reproducible by outside bodies.
It's not independently assessed, such as all the Medicare attributable laboratories in Australia
where you have an outside party like Nata or the College of Pathologists coming.
And even the products that are produced in the labs in Australia are not available for others to sequence and check.
It really is what they say it is.
The ones that are overseas are even in a lot of ways less supervised than the ones in Australia.
But it's the same problem.
I remember about a decade ago when a lot of people, well, and still have chronic fatigue,
that tests were being sent over for rickettsia and a whole lot of those things.
And again, they were found, oh, this was rickettsia, but nobody else could reproduce the same results.
Now, again, we have to have an open mind.
Sometimes people can do things differently, and we need to learn from that.
But if we want to consistently find results that we believe,
they've got to be reducible, not only in the laboratory that's doing it,
but other independent laboratories should be able to get the same result,
and your results should be able to be checked by outside parties
to check that what you're saying is positive is truly positive.
But there are Borrelia species, in other words, the same family of bugs in Australia.
We've got our own versions of these.
Do they cause human disease?
Well, I think the honest answer is we don't know yet.
We have found some Borrelia.
They seem to be quite distantly related to Borrelia burgdorferi,
which causes Lyme disease and not really in exactly the same family.
But I think that means we need to be open-minded.
We need to have research done that looks like what's in ticks,
what's in animals, what's in people,
and then show one way or another by various things that,
well, yes, this person has got an infection,
we've found the DNA or we've found the antibodies,
and this is reproducible.
and also that it actually does appear to be producing some reproducible disease
